lesson.title: The Twisted Ladder: Architecture of the DNA Molecule
lesson.summary: The DNA double helix is the twisted, ladder-like structure formed by two antiparallel strands of nucleotides, held together by hydrogen bonds between bases and covalent bonds along each sugar-phosphate backbone, and this structure explains how DNA can store and faithfully copy genetic information.
lesson.body:
DNA structure begins with a single strand: a backbone of alternating sugar and phosphate groups, linked together by strong covalent bonds, with one of four nitrogenous bases, adenine, thymine, guanine, or cytosine, attached to each sugar. In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick proposed that DNA does not exist as a single strand but as two such strands wound around each other into a double helix, a model built directly on Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction images of DNA fibers, which revealed the molecule's helical, regularly repeating structure, and on Erwin Chargaff's earlier observation that the amount of adenine in DNA always closely matches the amount of thymine, and the amount of guanine always closely matches the amount of cytosine.

In the double helix, the two sugar-phosphate backbones run along the outside of the molecule, twisted around a shared central axis, while the nitrogenous bases point inward, toward each other, at the center. Each base on one strand forms hydrogen bonds with a specific base on the opposite strand, holding the two strands together along the molecule's entire length, discussed in full in the next chapter on base pairing rules. Hydrogen bonds are individually much weaker than the covalent bonds that link sugars to phosphates within a backbone, and that difference in bond strength is functionally important: the strong covalent backbone keeps each strand chemically intact, while the comparatively weak hydrogen bonds between strands allow the two strands of the helix to be separated relatively easily when a cell needs to copy or read the DNA, without breaking either backbone.

The two strands of the helix are also antiparallel, meaning they run in opposite chemical directions. Each strand has a distinct 5' end, where a free phosphate group is attached to the 5' carbon of the terminal sugar, and a distinct 3' end, where a free hydroxyl group is attached to the 3' carbon of the terminal sugar. If one strand of the double helix is oriented 5' to 3' reading left to right, the strand paired with it runs 3' to 5' reading in that same left to right direction. This antiparallel arrangement is not an arbitrary detail. It is required for the bases to align properly for hydrogen bonding across the width of the helix, and it becomes essential later on for understanding how DNA replication and transcription proceed, since the enzymes that build new strands can only add nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction.

Structurally, the standard right-handed double helix, called B-DNA, has a fairly uniform diameter of about 2 nanometers along its length, and it completes roughly one full turn approximately every 10 base pairs. Because the two backbones are not positioned directly opposite each other around the helix, the twisting creates two grooves of different sizes running along the outside of the molecule, called the major groove and minor groove, which give proteins that regulate or interact with DNA a way to read the sequence of bases without having to unwind the helix. This elegant structure, two complementary strands wound around each other, is what allows DNA to do the two things a hereditary molecule most needs to do: store information stably in the sequence of bases, and make that information easy to copy accurately, since each strand already carries within it, through base pairing, the complete instructions for reconstructing its partner.
